adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The lighthouse at Ardmore Point had stood for a hundred and forty years, and in that time its keepers had written down every repair, every storm and every visitor. Maren found the first volume in a tin box beneath the stairs, its pages swollen with damp and its ink faded to a brown whisper. She carried it to the kitchen table and began to read.

The entries for the early years were short and practical. A lamp was cleaned. A hinge was oiled. A pane was replaced after a gull flew into it. The keepers wrote in a cramped hand, as if paper cost more than it did, and they rarely named themselves.

By the middle of the volume the handwriting changed. A new keeper had arrived, a man who signed himself only as T. He was fond of detail. He recorded the direction of the wind at dawn, the colour of the sea at dusk, the number of ships that passed beyond the reef. He noted that the brass fittings were polished on Sundays and that the stair treads were scrubbed on the first Monday of every month.

Maren read on through a long winter of gales. T. described a night when the light failed and he climbed the tower twice to relight the burner, his hands numb and the ladder slick with spray. He described the morning afterward, when the sea lay flat and grey and the gulls came back to the rocks as though nothing had happened. He described the supply boat arriving late with flour and paraffin and a letter from his sister that he did not open for a week.

In the spring the first volume ended, and Maren closed it and sat for a while listening to the kettle. Then she opened the second volume, and the story continued as if no time had passed at all. T. was still there. The wind still came from the west. The brass still shone on Sundays.

It was near the end of the second volume that she found the entry that made her stop. T. had written it in a shaking hand, late at night, after the weather had turned. He recorded that the lens had cracked along its lower edge, that he had sent for a new one, and that until it arrived he would polish the old one every evening and hope the crack held. Three days later he added a single line: the crack had widened, and he had polished the lens again by the light of a candle, and the beam was still true.

Maren read the line twice. Then she went to the window and looked out at the point, where the tower stood exactly as it had stood for a hundred and forty years, and she wondered what it had cost a man to write so little about so much, and whether anyone had ever answered his letter.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context positive holdout: a ~500-token narrative in which the repeat markers (' twice', ' back', ' later', ' again', ' second', ' replaced') sit deep in the passage rather than in the opening words, testing whether the pole still reads the feature in a long document.
